title: The Arabic Feature in the Neuron Basis
takeaway: The Arabic script feature's direction, written out one MLP neuron at a time, is spread across many neurons rather than living in one: 27 of the 512 coefficients have magnitude at least 0.1, and the three largest are negative. The paper reads this as evidence that dictionary learning did not simply rediscover an already-clean neuron.
walkthrough:
This is a stem plot of one vector. The vector is the dictionary direction for the [[arabic-script-feature]], A/1/3450, written out coordinate by coordinate.

That vector lives in the MLP activation space of the [[one-layer-transformer-testbed]], which has 512 neurons. So it has 512 numbers in it. The x-axis runs from 0 to 512 and each thin stem is one neuron. The y-axis, "Weight Value", is that neuron's coefficient. Blue stems rise above zero, red stems fall below it.

The numbers come from the autoencoder's decoder column for feature 3450. Columns of the [[dictionary-decoder]] are the [[feature-direction]]s, and each column is held at [[unit-norm-dictionary-columns]] — L2 length exactly 1. That constraint gives you a yardstick: the 512 squared coefficients must sum to 1.

So, two reference points for reading the plot. If the feature were one neuron under a new name, a single stem would sit at $\pm 1$ and every other stem would be flat at zero. If the feature were spread perfectly evenly, every stem would be $1/\sqrt{512} \approx 0.044$.

Neither happens. The tallest stem is about $0.2$ in magnitude, so that one neuron accounts for $0.2^2 = 0.04$ — about four percent of the vector's squared length. Twenty-seven neurons reach magnitude $0.1$; each of those contributes at least $0.01$, so together they hold at least $0.27$ of the length. Roughly a quarter of the vector sits in about five percent of the neurons. Distributed, then, but heavy-tailed rather than flat — which is what a [[privileged-basis]] would predict.

Now the signs. The three largest coefficients by magnitude are all negative, which the paper flags with an exclamation mark and does not explain. MLP activations are post-ReLU and non-negative, so the strongest thing this feature does in the neuron basis is subtract. Searching for neurons that light up on Arabic would never surface them. Consistent with that, a scan of every neuron's top 20 dataset examples ([[top-dataset-example-search]]) turns up one neuron with a single Arabic example.

The plot alone does not rule out that these coefficients cancel so as to sharpen one neuron. The paper tests that separately, via the [[most-correlated-neuron]], and concludes the feature is [[feature-neuron-nonalignment]].

terms.definition: The plot's title. "Dictionary vector" is this paper's name for one column of the sparse autoencoder's decoder matrix $W_d$, and the "weights" are that column's 512 entries.
The identifier of the feature being plotted, under the paper's naming scheme: transformer "A", dictionary learning run "1", feature number 3450 in that run. Here it names the Arabic script feature.
The coefficient of a single neuron in the feature's dictionary vector — how much of that neuron's activation the feature writes when it fires. Signed, so it can be negative.
The position within the 512-entry dictionary vector. Because the autoencoder reconstructs MLP activations, position $i$ is MLP neuron $i$ of transformer A.
Neurons with a positive coefficient: when the feature fires, it adds to these neurons' activations. The tallest reaches roughly +0.16.
Neurons with a negative coefficient: the feature subtracts from these. The three largest coefficients by magnitude in the whole vector are of this kind.
The coordinate system in which each axis is one MLP neuron. Writing a feature in this basis asks how much of it each individual neuron carries.
A direction in activation space that the sparse autoencoder learned, meant to correspond to one interpretable thing the model tracks — here, text in Arabic script.
The unit-length column of the decoder along which a feature writes into activation space when it is active. This plot is one such column, unrolled.
A single entry of the dictionary vector. Its magnitude says how much of the feature's direction lies along that neuron; its sign says which way.
The horizontal axis at weight 0. Most of the 512 neurons sit visibly close to it, which is why the vector reads as spiky rather than dense.
The writing system used by Arabic, Farsi, Urdu and others. This feature's hypothesized trigger is text written in it, not any one language.

numbers.meaning: The number of stems, and the number of neurons in transformer A's MLP layer. The autoencoder reconstructs those 512 MLP activations, so every dictionary vector has 512 entries.
The x-axis ticks — neuron indices, in steps of 64. They are just labels for position; neuron ordering carries no meaning, so nothing should be read into where the tall stems fall.

The y-axis ticks, in steps of 0.05. (The rendered image prints the -0.10 tick as "-0.01", which looks like a rendering slip: it sits between -0.05 and -0.15.) The visible range is roughly +0.16 down to -0.20.
The count of neurons whose coefficient is at least 0.1 in magnitude — the paper's headline number for this plot, and its measure of how many neurons the feature meaningfully uses.

The magnitude threshold the paper chose for counting a neuron as a real contributor. It is arbitrary, but it is over twice the 0.044 you would see if the feature were spread evenly, so a coefficient above it is a genuine participant rather than noise.
How many of the largest-magnitude coefficients are negative: all of the top three. This is the sign observation, marked in the text with an exclamation mark and left unexplained.
The magnitude of the single largest coefficient (a negative one). Compare with 1.0, which is what a one-neuron feature would show; this neuron carries about 4% of the vector's squared length.
The L2 norm every decoder column is constrained to. It is what makes the coefficients comparable across features, and it is why the 512 squared coefficients sum to 1.
The coefficient every neuron would have if a unit-length feature were spread perfectly evenly across all 512. The reference point for calling this vector heavy-tailed rather than uniform.
The lower bound on the squared length held by the 27 large coefficients: 27 entries times at least $0.1^2 = 0.01$ each. Over a quarter of the vector, in about 5% of the neurons.

From the surrounding text, not the plot: scanning every neuron's top 20 dataset examples for Arabic script turns up exactly one neuron, with one Arabic example; eighteen of its remaining examples are English and one is Cyrillic. A second, independent check that no neuron encodes this feature.

The number of dataset examples over which the paper computes activation correlations to find the neuron most correlated with the feature — the follow-up test that rules out the cancellation story this plot cannot rule out.
That most-correlated neuron. It responds to a mixture of non-English languages rather than to Arabic specifically, which the paper reads as superposition of mutually exclusive languages.
